precedents.name: Network Time Protocol (NTP), version 4
precedents.standard: RFC 5905, Section 6 (the 64-bit timestamp format), Section 7.3 (packet header variables) and Section 8 (on-wire protocol)

sends.what: the client's send time of the request, returned to it
the time the request arrived at the server
the time the response left the server

precedents.split: The client records the reply's arrival T4 itself and computes the round-trip delay as (T4 - T1) - (T3 - T2): the server's hold T3 - T2 is taken out, and each difference is on one clock, so no shared clock is needed. The offset, 1/2 [(T2 - T1) + (T3 - T4)], comes from the same four times.

evidence.quote: Origin Timestamp (org): Time at the client when the request departed for the server, in NTP timestamp format.
Receive Timestamp (rec): Time at the server when the request arrived from the client, in NTP timestamp format.
Transmit Timestamp (xmt): Time at the server when the response left for the client, in NTP timestamp format.
Destination Timestamp (dst): Time at the client when the reply arrived from the server, in NTP timestamp format.
It includes a 32-bit unsigned seconds field spanning 136 years and a 32-bit fraction field resolving 232 picoseconds.

The four most recent timestamps, T1 through T4, are used to compute the offset of B relative to A theta = T(B) - T(A) = 1/2 * [(T2-T1) + (T3-T4)] and the round-trip delay delta = T(ABA) = (T4-T1) - (T3-T2).

precedents.name: ICMP Timestamp and Timestamp Reply
precedents.standard: RFC 792, 'Timestamp or Timestamp Reply Message'

sends.what: the time the sender last touched the request before sending it, returned to it
the time the echoer first touched the request on receipt
the time the echoer last touched the reply on sending it

precedents.split: RFC 792 defines the three times and refers their use to Mills; it states no formula. From the definitions, the echoer's hold is the Transmit less the Receive Timestamp, both on the echoer's clock, and the requester can take it out of its round trip without a shared clock.

evidence.quote: The timestamp is 32 bits of milliseconds since midnight UT.

The Originate Timestamp is the time the sender last touched the message before sending it, the Receive Timestamp is the time the echoer first touched it on receipt, and the Transmit Timestamp is the time the echoer last touched the message on sending it.

If the time is not available in miliseconds or cannot be provided with respect to midnight UT then any time can be inserted in a timestamp provided the high order bit of the timestamp is also set to indicate this non-standard value.
One use of these timestamps is described by Mills [5].

precedents.name: ICMP Echo and Echo Reply (ping)
precedents.standard: RFC 792, 'Echo or Echo Reply Message'

sends.what: whatever the sender put in the echo request, returned unchanged
sends.clock: the sender's, if it put a time in the data; the echoer adds none

precedents.split: Carries none: the echoer returns the sender's data and adds no time of its own, so the round trip the sender measures includes the echoer's turnaround.

evidence.quote: The data received in the echo message must be returned in the echo reply message.
However, the most common facility for round-trip measurements is the ICMP Echo Request/Reply (used by the ping tool), and issues with this method are documented in Section 2.6 of [RFC2681].

precedents.name: RTCP sender and receiver reports (LSR and DLSR)
precedents.standard: RFC 3550, Section 6.4.1 (sender report and reception report blocks)

sends.what: the wallclock time the sender report was sent
the middle 32 bits of the NTP timestamp of the last sender report received, returned to its sender
the time between receiving that sender report and sending this reception report block

precedents.split: The media sender records the arrival time A of a reception report and computes the round trip as A - LSR - DLSR: LSR is its own earlier time and DLSR is the receiver's hold, measured on the receiver's clock, so no shared clock is needed.

evidence.quote: NTP timestamp: 64 bits Indicates the wallclock time (see Section 4) when this report was sent so that it may be used in combination with timestamps returned in reception reports from other receivers to measure round-trip propagation to those receivers.
last SR timestamp (LSR): 32 bits The middle 32 bits out of 64 in the NTP timestamp (as explained in Section 4) received as part of the most recent RTCP sender report (SR) packet from source SSRC_n.
delay since last SR (DLSR): 32 bits The delay, expressed in units of 1/65536 seconds, between receiving the last SR packet from source SSRC_n and sending this reception report block.
It calculates the total round-trip time A-LSR using the last SR timestamp (LSR) field, and then subtracting this field to leave the round-trip propagation delay as (A - LSR - DLSR).

precedents.name: RTCP Extended Reports: Receiver Reference Time and DLRR blocks
precedents.standard: RFC 3611, Sections 4.4 and 4.5

sends.what: the time the block was sent by a participant that sends no media
the middle 32 bits of that NTP timestamp, returned
the time between receiving the Receiver Reference Time block and sending the DLRR block

precedents.split: The same arithmetic as RTCP's receiver reports, for a participant that sends no media: it sends its own timestamp, and takes the far end's hold (DLRR) out of the time since that timestamp to get its round trip.

evidence.quote: This block extends RTCP's timestamp reporting so that non-senders may also send timestamps.
A non-sender may estimate its round trip time (RTT) to other participants, as proposed in [18], by sending this report block and receiving DLRR Report Blocks (see next section) in reply.

last RR timestamp (LRR): 32 bits The middle 32 bits out of 64 in the NTP timestamp (as explained in the previous section), received as part of a Receiver Reference Time Report Block from participant SSRC_n.

delay since last RR (DLRR): 32 bits The delay, expressed in units of 1/65536 seconds, between receiving the last Receiver Reference Time Report Block from participant SSRC_n and sending this DLRR Report Block.

precedents.name: RTCP congestion control feedback (per-packet arrival times)
precedents.standard: RFC 8888, Section 3.1

sends.field: Arrival time offset (ATO), per RTP packet
sends.what: the packet's arrival at the receiver, as an offset before the Report Timestamp
the instant the report is reporting on, from which the offsets are counted
sends.clock: receiver (the clock of its sender-report NTP timestamps)
sends.resolution: 1/65536 s (middle 32 bits of an NTP timestamp)

precedents.split: For every RTP packet the receiver reports when it arrived, as RTS less ATO on the receiver's own clock, for use in congestion control. RFC 8888 defines no round-trip computation from these fields; the arrival times are on the receiver's clock only.

evidence.quote: Arrival time offset (ATO, 13 bits): The arrival time of the RTP packet at the receiver, as an offset before the time represented by the Report Timestamp (RTS) field of this RTCP congestion control feedback report. The ATO field is in units of 1/1024 seconds

The RTCP congestion control feedback report packet concludes with the Report Timestamp field (RTS, 32 bits). This denotes the time instant on which this packet is reporting and is the instant from which the arrival time offset values are calculated.

The value of the RTS field is derived from the same clock used to generate the NTP timestamp field in RTCP Sender Report (SR) packets. It is formatted as the middle 32 bits of an NTP format timestamp, as described in Section 4 of [RFC3550].

precedents.name: SIP Timestamp header
precedents.standard: RFC 3261, Sections 8.2.6.1 and 20.38, and the Timestamp rule of the ABNF in Section 25.1

sends.what: when the UAC sent the request, copied into the response
sends.resolution: decimal number with an optional fraction

sends.what: the time between the UAS receiving the request and sending the response
sends.resolution: seconds, decimal with an optional fraction

precedents.split: A UAS that delays its response adds the delay value, its hold of the request in seconds on its own clock, to the Timestamp it returns, and the UAC can subtract it from its round trip. RFC 3261 states the rule for 100 (Trying) responses and leaves the use for RTT estimates to extensions and applications.

evidence.quote: When a 100 (Trying) response is generated, any Timestamp header field present in the request MUST be copied into this 100 (Trying) response.

If there is a delay in generating the response, the UAS SHOULD add a delay value into the Timestamp value in the response. This value MUST contain the difference between the time of sending of the response and receipt of the request, measured in seconds.
The Timestamp header field describes when the UAC sent the request to the UAS.
Although there is no normative behavior defined here that makes use of the header, it allows for extensions or SIP applications to obtain RTT estimates.
Timestamp = "Timestamp" HCOLON 1*(DIGIT) [ "." *(DIGIT) ] [ LWS delay ] delay = *(DIGIT) [ "." *(DIGIT) ]

precedents.name: Two-Way Active Measurement Protocol (TWAMP)
precedents.standard: RFC 5357, Sections 1, 4.2 and 4.2.1; timestamp format of RFC 4656, Section 4.1.2; the PTP format option of RFC 8186

sends.what: the time the test packet was received by the reflector
sends.resolution: NTP 64-bit format (2^-32 s), or PTPv2 truncated format when the Z bit is set

sends.what: the reflector's transmit time of the reflected packet
a copy of the sender's transmit time
the reflector's estimate of its timestamps' error and whether its clock is synchronized

precedents.split: The reflector stamps the test packet's arrival and its own transmission; the difference, the time the packet spent in the reflector, comes out of the round trip, which needs no synchronized clocks.

evidence.quote: TWAMP employs time stamps applied at the echo destination (reflector) to enable greater accuracy (processing delays can be accounted for).
Two-way measurements are common in IP networks, primarily because synchronization between local and remote clocks is unnecessary for round-trip delay

Prior to the transmission of the test packet, the Session-Reflector MUST enter the best possible approximation of its actual sending time as its Timestamp (in the packet). This permits the determination of the elapsed time between the reception of the packet and its transmission.

Receive Timestamp is the time the test packet was received by the reflector. The difference between Timestamp and Receive Timestamp is the amount of time the packet was in transition in the Session- Reflector.

Timestamp and Error Estimate are the Session-Reflector's transmit timestamp and error estimate for the reflected test packet, respectively. The format of all timestamp and error estimate fields follow the definition and formats defined by OWAMP, Section 4.1.2 in [RFC4656].
o 0 - NTP 64-bit format of a timestamp. o 1 - PTPv2-truncated format of a timestamp.

precedents.name: Simple Two-way Active Measurement Protocol (STAMP)
precedents.standard: RFC 8762, Sections 4.2.1 and 4.3.1

sends.what: the time the test packet was received by the Session-Reflector
sends.resolution: NTP 64-bit format (2^-32 s) by default; PTPv2 truncated format if configured (Z field)

sends.what: the time taken by the Session-Reflector at the start of transmitting the reflected packet
a copy of the sender's timestamp

precedents.split: As in TWAMP: the sender takes the reflector's hold, Timestamp less Receive Timestamp, out of the round trip, with no shared clock.

evidence.quote: Receive Timestamp is the time the test packet was received by the Session-Reflector. Timestamp is the time taken by the Session-Reflector at the start of transmitting the test packet.
The Timestamp field is eight octets long. The STAMP node MUST support the Network Time Protocol (NTP) version 4 64-bit timestamp format [RFC5905], the format used in [RFC5357].
The Z field is interpreted as it is defined in Section 2.3 of [RFC8186]: 0: NTP 64-bit format of a timestamp 1: PTPv2 truncated format of a timestamp
The Session-Sender Sequence Number, Session-Sender Timestamp, and Session-Sender Error Estimate fields are copies of the corresponding fields in the STAMP-Test packet sent by the Session- Sender.

precedents.name: One-Way Active Measurement Protocol (OWAMP)
precedents.standard: RFC 4656, Sections 3.9 (Fetch-Session records) and 4.1.2 (timestamp and error estimate formats)

sends.what: the sender's transmit time of the test packet
the receiver's time of receipt, returned in the session's packet records
whether each party's clock is synchronized to UTC from an external source

precedents.split: Carries no hold: one-way delay is the receiver's receive time less the sender's send time, on two clocks, usable only when the clocks are synchronized, which the error estimate's S bit reports.

evidence.quote: Each packet record is 25 octets and includes 4 octets of sequence number, 8 octets of send timestamp, 2 octets of send timestamp error estimate, 8 octets of receive timestamp, 2 octets of receive timestamp error estimate, and 1 octet of Time To Live (TTL), or Hop Limit in IPv6:

The format of the timestamp is the same as in [RFC1305] and is as follows: the first 32 bits represent the unsigned integer number of seconds elapsed since 0h on 1 January 1900; the next 32 bits represent the fractional part of a second that has elapsed since then.
The first bit, S, SHOULD be set if the party generating the timestamp has a clock that is synchronized to UTC using an external source

Although OWAMP is often run on hosts with well-synchronized clocks, it is also possible to run it on hosts with clocks completely untrained. The delays obtained thus are, of course, not directly usable;

precedents.name: MPLS delay measurement
precedents.standard: RFC 6374, Sections 2.4, 3.2 and 9.2

sends.what: the querier's transmit time, returned
sends.resolution: NTP 64-bit format or truncated IEEE 1588v2 PTP format, as the timestamp format fields say

sends.what: the time the query was received at the responder
the time the responder transmits the response

precedents.split: The querier records T4 and computes the two-way channel delay as (T4 - T1) - (T3 - T2), the responder's hold taken out, with no synchronized clocks; one-way values need synchronized clocks.

evidence.quote: Measurement of the one-way delay quantities requires that the clocks of A and B be synchronized, whereas the two-way delay metrics can be measured directly even when this is not the case (provided A and B have stable clocks).

When the query is received at B, Timestamp 2 is set to T2. At this point, B copies Timestamp 1 to Timestamp 3 and Timestamp 2 to Timestamp 4, and re-initializes Timestamp 1 and Timestamp 2 to 0. When B transmits the response, Timestamp 1 is set to T3.
At this point, A can compute the two-way channel delay associated with the channel as two-way channel delay = (T4 - T1) - (T3 - T2) and the round-trip delay as round-trip delay = T4 - T1.
2 Network Time Protocol version 4 64-bit 64 RFC 6374 Timestamp 3 Truncated IEEE 1588v2 PTP Timestamp 64 RFC 6374

precedents.name: Precision Time Protocol (IEEE 1588), as implemented by linuxptp
precedents.standard: IEEE 1588-2008 (not freely published); message layouts and arithmetic as implemented in linuxptp v4.4 (msg.h, ddt.h, port.c, tc.c, tsproc.c)

sends.what: the time the master received the slave's Delay_Req
the time the peer received the Pdelay_Req
the time the peer sent the Pdelay_Resp
residence times added by each transparent clock the message crossed; in a one-step peer delay response, the responder's turnaround
sends.clock: each transparent clock or responder that adds to it

precedents.split: In the peer delay exchange the responder sends the time it received the request and the time it sent the response (or their difference in the correction field), and the requester computes the link delay as ((t2 - t3) + (t4 - t1)) / 2, the responder's turnaround taken out, with no shared clock. Transparent clocks add each message's residence time in them to the correction field, which the receiver subtracts, so time queued in a switch comes out too.
precedents.note: The IEEE standard itself is not public; the fields and the arithmetic are cited from linuxptp's source, pinned to its tag v4.4 on the project's GitHub repository. The reading that a one-step peer delay response carries the turnaround in its correction field rests on port.c, which sets t2 and t3 to zero for such a response and adds the correction to t3.

evidence.quote: struct delay_resp_msg { struct ptp_header hdr; struct Timestamp receiveTimestamp; struct PortIdentity requestingPortIdentity; uint8_t suffix[0]; } PACKED;
struct pdelay_resp_msg { struct ptp_header hdr; struct Timestamp requestReceiptTimestamp; struct PortIdentity requestingPortIdentity; uint8_t suffix[0]; } PACKED;
struct pdelay_resp_fup_msg { struct ptp_header hdr; struct Timestamp responseOriginTimestamp; struct PortIdentity requestingPortIdentity; uint8_t suffix[0]; } PACKED;
Octet flagField[2]; Integer64 correction; UInteger32 reserved2;
typedef Integer64 TimeInterval; /* nanoseconds << 16 */
struct Timestamp { uint16_t seconds_msb; /* 16 bits + */ uint32_t seconds_lsb; /* 32 bits = 48 bits*/ UInteger32 nanoseconds; } PACKED;

t3c = tmv_add(t3, tmv_add(c1, c2));
c1 = net2host64(resp->header.correction); c2 = c1 + tmv_to_TimeInterval(residence); resp->header.correction = host2net64(c2);

precedents.name: QUIC ACK Delay
precedents.standard: RFC 9000, Sections 13.2.5, 18.2 and 19.3; RFC 9002, Sections 5.2 and 5.3

sends.what: the delay the acknowledging endpoint introduced on purpose between receiving the largest acknowledged packet and sending the ACK
sends.resolution: microseconds times 2^ack_delay_exponent (default exponent 3, so 8 us units)

precedents.split: The sender subtracts the peer's ACK Delay, capped at max_ack_delay once the handshake is confirmed, from its RTT sample, unless that would take the sample below min_rtt; min_rtt itself uses local times only. The field covers only delays the peer controls, not time the packet waited in its kernel.

evidence.quote: An endpoint measures the delays intentionally introduced between the time the packet with the largest packet number is received and the time an acknowledgment is sent. The endpoint encodes this acknowledgment delay in the ACK Delay field of an ACK frame; see Section 19.3.

A packet might be held in the OS kernel or elsewhere on the host before being processed. An endpoint MUST NOT include delays that it does not control when populating the ACK Delay field in an ACK frame.

ACK Delay: A variable-length integer encoding the acknowledgment delay in microseconds; see Section 13.2.5. It is decoded by multiplying the value in the field by 2 to the power of the ack_delay_exponent transport parameter sent by the sender of the ACK frame; see Section 18.2.
If this value is absent, a default value of 3 is assumed (indicating a multiplier of 8). Values above 20 are invalid.
adjusted_rtt = latest_rtt if (latest_rtt >= min_rtt + ack_delay): adjusted_rtt = latest_rtt - ack_delay
MUST NOT subtract the acknowledgment delay from the RTT sample if the resulting value is smaller than the min_rtt.
An endpoint uses only locally observed times in computing the min_rtt and does not adjust for acknowledgment delays reported by the peer.

precedents.name: TCP Timestamps option
precedents.standard: RFC 7323, Sections 3, 4 and 5.4

sends.what: the current value of the sending TCP's timestamp clock
sends.resolution: 1 ms to 1 s per tick (the RFC's chosen range)

sends.what: a TSval received from the other end, echoed
sends.clock: the other end (its own value, returned)

precedents.split: Carries no hold: the receiver echoes a TSval and sends no time of its own that the other end can relate to it. With delayed ACKs the RFC wants the measured RTT to include the delay, so the receiver echoes the TSval of the earliest unacknowledged segment.

evidence.quote: The Timestamps option carries two four-byte timestamp fields. The TSval field contains the current value of the timestamp clock of the TCP sending the option.
These TSval values are echoed in TSecr values in the reverse direction. The difference between a received TSecr value and the current timestamp clock value provides an RTT measurement.

The data-sender TCP must measure the effective RTT, including the additional time due to delayed ACKs, or else it will retransmit unnecessarily. Thus, when delayed ACKs are in use, the receiver SHOULD reply with the TSval field from the earliest unacknowledged segment.
Based upon these considerations, we choose a timestamp clock frequency in the range 1 ms to 1 sec per tick.
The receiver treats the timestamp value as simply a monotonically non-decreasing serial number, without any connection to time.

precedents.name: HTTP/2 PING frame
precedents.standard: RFC 9113, Section 6.7

sends.what: the sender's payload, returned unchanged
sends.clock: the sender's, if it put a time in it; the receiver adds none

precedents.split: Carries none: the receiver returns the payload and is asked to answer before any other frame, so the measured round trip includes its turnaround.

evidence.quote: The PING frame (type=0x06) is a mechanism for measuring a minimal round-trip time from the sender, as well as determining whether an idle connection is still functional.

Receivers of a PING frame that does not include an ACK flag MUST send a PING frame with the ACK flag set in response, with an identical frame payload. PING responses SHOULD be given higher priority than any other frame.

precedents.name: gRPC over HTTP/2
precedents.standard: gRPC, doc/PROTOCOL-HTTP2.md, 'Responses' (release v1.85.0)

sends.what: application-defined response headers and trailers; the protocol defines no time field in a response

precedents.split: Carries none: a response's headers and trailers hold the status, the encodings and custom metadata, so any server time is an application's own metadata.

evidence.quote: **Response-Headers** → HTTP-Status [Message-Encoding] [Message-Accept-Encoding] Content-Type \*Custom-Metadata
**Trailers** → Status [Status-Message] [Status-Details] \*Custom-Metadata

precedents.name: HTTP Server-Timing header (W3C Server Timing)
precedents.standard: W3C Server Timing, Working Draft of 7 April 2026, Sections 2 and 3.2

sends.what: a duration the server chose to report for the request-response cycle, under a metric name of its own
sends.resolution: a decimal number, milliseconds by recommendation

sends.what: a description of the metric

precedents.split: A server can report durations it measured, such as its own processing of the request, and a client can subtract them from its round trip; the specification defines no standard metric for the server's hold, so each metric means what the server says it does.

evidence.quote: The Server-Timing header field is used to communicate one or more metrics and descriptions for the given request-response cycle.
This specification establishes the server-timing-params for server-timing-param-names "dur" for duration and "desc" for description , both optional.

Since duration is a DOMHighResTimeStamp , it usually represents a duration in milliseconds. Since this is not enforceable in practice, duration can represent any unit of time, and having it represent a duration in milliseconds is a recommendation.

precedents.name: Amazon CloudFront's Server-Timing metrics
precedents.standard: Amazon CloudFront Developer Guide, 'Understand response headers policies', section 'Server-Timing header' (as retrieved 27 October 2026)

sends.what: the time from the edge location finishing receiving the request to its sending the first byte of the response
the time from the origin request being completed to the first byte of the origin's response

precedents.split: With the setting on (it is off unless a response headers policy enables it, for a sampled share of responses), a viewer can subtract cdn-downstream-fbl, the edge's hold from receiving the request to sending the first byte, measured on the edge's clock, from its own round trip.

evidence.quote: Use the Server-Timing header setting to enable the Server-Timing header in HTTP responses sent from CloudFront.
cdn-downstream-fbl Contains a value with the number of milliseconds between when the edge location finished receiving the request and when it sent the first byte of the response to the viewer.

cdn-upstream-fbl Contains a value with the number of milliseconds between when the origin HTTP request is completed and when the first byte is received in the response from the origin (first byte latency).
The sampling rate is a number 0–100 (inclusive) that specifies the percentage of responses that you want CloudFront to add the Server-Timing header to.

precedents.name: Envoy's x-envoy-upstream-service-time response header
precedents.standard: Envoy documentation, router filter, 'HTTP response headers set on downstream responses' (source of release v1.40.2)

sends.what: the time the upstream host spent processing the request plus the network latency between Envoy and the upstream host

precedents.split: A client can subtract it from its round trip to leave the path between itself and Envoy plus Envoy's own handling; it is Envoy's round trip to the upstream, network included, not the upstream's hold alone.

evidence.quote: Contains the time in milliseconds spent by the upstream host processing the request and the network latency between Envoy and upstream host. This is useful if the client wants to determine service time compared to network latency between client and Envoy. This header is set on responses.

precedents.name: Rack's x-runtime response header
precedents.standard: Rack v3.2.6, lib/rack/runtime.rb (the Rack::Runtime middleware)

sends.what: the time the wrapped application took over the request, measured around the call inside the server process
sends.resolution: seconds printed with six decimals (1 us)

precedents.split: A client can subtract it from its round trip; what remains includes the network, the server's queues and every layer outside the middleware.

evidence.quote: # Sets an "x-runtime" response header, indicating the response # time of the request, in seconds
FORMAT_STRING = "%0.6f" # :nodoc:
start_time = Utils.clock_time _, headers, _ = response = @app.call(env) request_time = Utils.clock_time - start_time

precedents.name: Request-start header of web routers (X-Request-Start, X-Queue-Start)
precedents.standard: Heroku Dev Center, 'HTTP Routing', 'Heroku Headers'; nginx ngx_http_core_module, variable $msec; newrelic-ruby-agent 10.9.1, queue_time.rb; Datadog dd-trace-rb v2.47.0, request_queue.rb

sends.what: the time the router or proxy received the request, added to the request it forwards to the application
sends.resolution: Heroku: Unix time in ms; nginx with $msec: seconds with ms resolution; Apache: microseconds

precedents.split: The stamp travels forward to the application, not back to the client. The application's performance-monitoring library subtracts it from its own clock reading to report the request's queueing between router and application, which needs the two hosts' clocks to agree; both libraries read drop or zero a negative result.

precedents.name: HTTP Age header
precedents.standard: RFC 9111, Sections 4.2.3 and 5.1

sends.what: the sender's estimate of the time since the response was generated or validated at the origin; each cache adds the time the response stayed with it and the round trip of its own request
sends.clock: each cache in turn, as a duration

precedents.split: A client learns how long the response has been held along the path, in whole seconds; it is a stay of the response in caches, not a hold of the client's own request.

evidence.quote: The "Age" response header field conveys the sender's estimate of the time since the response was generated or successfully validated at the origin server.
The Age field value is a non-negative integer, representing time in seconds (see Section 1.2.2).
apparent_age = max(0, response_time - date_value); response_delay = response_time - request_time; corrected_age_value = age_value + response_delay;
resident_time = now - response_time; current_age = corrected_initial_age + resident_time;

precedents.name: In Situ OAM (IOAM) trace data
precedents.standard: RFC 9197, Sections 4.4 and 4.4.2.3 to 4.4.2.5

sends.what: the time the packet was received by the node
the time the packet spent in the transit node

precedents.split: Each node can write into the packet the time it received it and the time the packet spent in it, and the data travels with the packet to the node that removes it, so each node's transit delay, on that node's clock, can be taken out of the path's delay; times written by different nodes need synchronized clocks to compare.

evidence.quote: The "timestamp seconds" field is a 4-octet unsigned integer field. It contains the absolute timestamp in seconds that specifies the time at which the packet was received by the node.
This field has three possible formats, based on either the Precision Time Protocol (PTP) (see e.g., [RFC8877]), NTP [RFC5905], or POSIX [POSIX].
An IOAM decapsulating node removes IOAM-Option-Type(s) from packets.

The "transit delay" field is a 4-octet unsigned integer in the range 0 to 2^31-1. It is the time in nanoseconds the packet spent in the transit node. This can serve as an indication of the queuing delay at the node.

Time of day when the packet was processed by the node, as well as the transit delay. Different definitions of processing time are feasible and expected, though it is important that all devices of an IOAM-Domain follow the same definition.

precedents.name: Apache Kafka's ThrottleTimeMs
precedents.standard: Apache Kafka 4.4.0, clients/src/main/resources/common/message/ProduceResponse.json

sends.what: the duration for which the request was throttled because of a quota violation, or zero

precedents.split: A duration the broker measures and sends in the produce response, but it reports quota throttling only, not the broker's hold of the request, so it does not let a producer split its round trip.
precedents.note: Kafka is one of the brokers coded in the audit; the field is recorded here because it is a broker-side duration sent in a response.

precedents.name: Informatica Ultra Messaging, streaming (high-resolution and receive timestamps)
precedents.standard: Ultra Messaging 6.17.2 Concepts Guide, 'High-resolution Timestamps'; UM C API 6.17.2, lbm_msg_t_stct

sends.what: the time the subscriber's own network card received the message's packet (LBT-RM on Solarflare cards with Onload)
the time the publisher's own network card transmitted the message's packet, with the message's sequence number, delivered to the publisher
the earliest time the message was received, up to 500 ms before its actual receipt
sends.resolution: seconds and microseconds; accurate only to 500 ms

precedents.split: Each end learns only its own times: the publisher its transmit time, the subscriber its receive time. Neither travels to the other end, so no far-end time or hold reaches either side; a one-way latency needs the application to carry the transmit time across, on clocks the network cards synchronize by PTP.
precedents.note: The streaming core is brokerless (peer-to-peer); Ultra Messaging's persistent Store is coded among the brokers (batch_08.json).

evidence.quote: Ultra Messaging (Version 6.17.2) Concepts Guide

The Ultra Messaging (UM) high-resolution message timestamp feature leverages the hardware timestamping function of certain Solarflare network interface cards (NICs) to measure sub-microsecond times that packets are transmitted and received.
For subscribers, each message's receive timestamp is delivered in the message's header structure (for C programs, lbm_msg_t field hr_timestamp , of type lbm_timespec_t ).
Each timestamp is a structure of 32 bits worth of seconds and 32 bits worth of nanoseconds.
For publishers, each message's transmit timestamp is delivered via the source event callback (for C programs, event type LBM_SRC_EVENT_TIMESTAMP).
Solarflare's NICs and Onload kernel-bypass driver implement PTP to synchronize timestamps across the network, allowing very accurate one-way latency measurements.

lbm_timeval_t tsp Timestamp indicating the earliest time that the message was received, in seconds and microseconds since midnight, January 1st, 1970 UTC. This time can be up to 500 milliseconds prior to actual receipt time
lbm_timespec_t hr_timestamp High Resolution Timestamp of the received message.
peer-to-peer design that removes messaging brokers and daemons for lower latency and higher reliability

precedents.name: Scalability protocols of nanomsg and NNG (request-reply header)
precedents.standard: NNG v2.0.0, docs/ref/proto/req.md; nanomsg 1.3.0, rfc/sp-request-reply-01.txt

sends.field: backtrace header: request ID and peer (channel) IDs
sends.what: 32-bit identifiers that route a reply back to its requester; no time

precedents.split: Carries none: the reply carries the request's header back and no time of the replier, so a requester's round trip includes the replier's turnaround.

evidence.quote: This protocol uses a {{ii:backtrace}} in the header. This form uses a stack of 32-bit big-endian identifiers.
There _must_ be at least one identifier, the **request ID**, which will be the last element in the array, and _must_ have the most significant bit set.
When a reply message is created, it is created using the same headers that the request contained.
Payload of the message is preceded by a stack of 32-bit tags.
As for the remaining 31 bits, they are either request ID (in the last tag) or a channel ID (in all the remaining tags).
